subject: Default log lifecycle: requests vs model outputs — operational summary and Qs
messages:
From: Sam Turner <sam.turner@acmehealth.com>
To: laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 28 Dec 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Clarify Redwood default log lifecycle for PII-sensitive flows

Hi Laura,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. Our security team asked for a short, concrete breakdown of Redwood's default "what we keep and for how long" for typical request/response interactions so we can map it to our data retention controls. A few specific asks: 

1) For a standard text-generation API call (prompt + model completion), what is kept by default immediately after the request completes? Please separate: raw request text, model outputs, streaming fragments (intermediate tokens), and any derived metadata (latency, token counts, model id).

2) What are the default retention windows (time-to-live) for each of the above tiers in the hosted product (US region)? We have customers who require 30-day max retention and need to know if that matches the default.

3) How is KV cache data treated? Is it persisted beyond the session boundary by default? If so, for how long?

4) What triggers an item to be removed ahead of TTL (customer erasure request, account deletion, etc.) and what is the typical evidence artifact Redwood provides to confirm deletion? Is there a standard export/proof-of-deletion record?

5) Any exceptions where certain fragments are retained longer for debugging/compliance (e.g., chargeable audit logs, anomaly investigations) and how those are scoped?

Can you send a concise summary we can attach to our internal control docs? Prefer a single page and a checklist for what customers need to request to get immediate erasure.

Appreciate it — Sam

--
Sam Turner
Senior Security Engineer
Acme Health
From: laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Sam Turner <sam.turner@acmehealth.com>
Cc: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Clarify Redwood default log lifecycle for PII-sensitive flows

Hi Sam — thanks for the clear list. Looping Kim (security/compliance) and Karthik (platform) to make sure the timelines are exact and we include the erasure runbook steps. Below is a concise operational breakdown; Kim and Karthik, please correct if I get any of the TTLs slightly off. I also attached a one-pager and a quick CSV checklist for an erasure request your ops team can use.

Summary (hosted, US region, default configuration):
- What we store immediately after a request: request body (prompt text), model outputs (final completion), request/response metadata (token counts, model version, latency), and short-lived diagnostic fragments for streamed responses when streaming is used.
- Storage tiers described as: transient buffer, session archive, artifact store.

High-level TTLs (defaults):
- Transient buffer (streamed token fragments and in-memory buffers): retained up to 48 hours, then automatically flushed unless persisted by a debug flag.
- Session archive (request + final model outputs + metadata): default 30 days.
- Artifact store (customer-uploaded files and attachments referenced by the session): retained per configured customer policy; default 90 days for hosted customers unless overridden by enterprise contract.

KV cache treatment: by default KV caches are ephemeral to the serving allocation and are drained within 24–72 hours of session inactivity; they are not persisted to long-term logs unless the customer explicitly enables session replay/audit mode.

Early removal triggers and evidence:
- Customer-initiated erasure: accept a verified request (support ticket + account owner confirmation). We queue a deletion job that purges session archive entries and returns a deletion confirmation ID.
- Account deletion/contract termination: full purge of session archives within the contract SLA (typically 14 days), artifacts handled per contract.
- Evidence: we provide a deletion confirmation token and a short audit log entry (ID, timestamp, scope) that customers can use as proof. We can also provide a manifest CSV listing deleted session IDs on request.

Exceptions:
- Short-term investigative retention: in rare cases (security incident, legal hold), a snapshot of relevant artifacts may be placed on a hold for investigation; such holds are subject to strict access controls and are scoped to specific session IDs with explicit retention end dates.

Next steps: Kim/Karthik — can you confirm the TTLs above and add any compliance wording for our SOC2/ISO attachments? Sam, if that summary looks good I can convert it into a single-page note you can attach to your control matrix.

Best,
Laura
VP, Solutions
Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood-data-lifecycle-one-pager.pdf
From: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>

Date: Wed, 30 Dec 2026 08:17:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Clarify Redwood default log lifecycle for PII-sensitive flows

Laura — thanks for the nicely formatted summary. A few clarifications to be explicit for Acme's control reviewers:

1) Precise default windows (hosted, us-east):
   - Stream buffer (intermediate streamed tokens): 0–48 hours. Buffers are ephemeral memory-backed fragments; they are only written to durable storage if a debug flag is set or a customer requests transcript persistence.
   - Session archive (request + final outputs + derived metadata): default TTL = 30 days. This is the baseline for hosted customers on standard plans.
   - Aggregated logs/operational metrics (anonymized token counts, system health telemetry): retained for 365 days by default for our operational observability; these are aggregated and do not contain PII by design.
   - Customer attachments and exports: 90 days by default unless an enterprise agreement shortens or extends that window.

2) KV caches: they are stored in-memory on serving nodes and are not part of the session archive by default. The cache eviction policy results in caches being drained within 24–72 hours of inactivity, and we do not persist cache contents to long-term logs.

3) Erasure workflow and proof:
   - Customer files a verified support request (support.redwood.ai ticket) and confirms account ownership.
   - We execute a scoped deletion job that removes session-archive records and, where applicable, associated artifacts.
   - Proof provided: deletion confirmation ID plus an audit manifest (CSV) listing deleted session IDs and timestamps. For enterprise contracts we can include signed deletion statements on company letterhead.

4) Holds & legal requests:
   - Holds require a legal or security escalation and are timeboxed with an explicit owner. We log hold creation and removal events; customers receive a copy of the hold manifest.

5) How to request immediate 30-day enforcement (for customers who must default to <=30 days):
   - Include a request in procurement or a support ticket referencing your account id and the desired default window. For self-serve accounts the 'data retention' toggle in the console can be used to set session archive TTL down to 7 days; enterprise accounts can lock a shorter default via contract addendum.

I'll add a short paragraph for SOC2 language about segregation and access controls before Laura packages this.

-Kim
Director, Security & Compliance
Redwood Inference
